**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** [A1]–[A2], $m>0$, the suppliers [F1]–[F9], and real Schwartz tests on $\mathbb R^2$.

1.1 Let $I=\mathbb N_0^2$, enumerated by total degree and lexicographic order. For each finite $F\subset I$, let $\mu_F$ have density $\prod_{\alpha\in F}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x_\alpha^2/2}$ on $\mathbb R^F$. [F5] makes these probability laws; integrating out coordinates with [F6] proves their consistency. Each coordinate space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is standard Borel by [F4]. Applying [F1] with [A1] yields $\Omega=\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder $\sigma$-algebra and a probability $\mathbb P$ having these finite marginals. The coordinate variables $\xi_\alpha(\omega)=\omega_\alpha$ are therefore independent standard normals. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, construct]

1.2 For $p\in\mathbb R^2$ put $w_m(p)=(|p|^2+m^2)^{-1/2}$. Since $m>0$, $w_m$ is smooth, and every derivative is bounded: its derivatives are finite sums of polynomial factors divided by positive powers of $|p|^2+m^2$, bounded near the origin and decaying at infinity. The product rule therefore shows multiplication by $w_m$ maps Schwartz space continuously to itself. Define $T_mf=\mathcal F_{2\pi}^{-1}\bigl(w_m(2\pi\cdot)\mathcal F_{2\pi}f\bigr)$. By [F8], $T_mf$ is Schwartz; because $w_m$ is real and even, $T_mf$ is real for real $f$. Under the exact convention in the Statement, $\widehat f(p)=\mathcal F_{2\pi}f(p/(2\pi))$, and the change of variables $p=2\pi\xi$ gives $\widehat{T_mf}(p)=w_m(p)\widehat f(p)$. [F7, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 For a finite initial segment $I_N$ of the fixed enumeration set $S_N=\sum_{\alpha\in I_N}(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\xi_\alpha^2$. The density in [F5] is normalized, and integration by parts using $(-xe^{-x^2/2})'=(x^2-1)e^{-x^2/2}$ gives $\mathbb E\xi_\alpha^2=1$. Hence $\mathbb E S_N=\sum_{\alpha\in I_N}(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\le\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)(n+1)^{-4}=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)^{-3}=:C<\infty$: grouping $n+1$ in dyadic blocks $[2^j,2^{j+1})$ bounds each block by $2^j2^{-3j}=2^{-2j}$, a summable geometric series. Markov's inequality, which follows from $\mathbf1_{\{S_N>M\}}\le S_N/M$, gives $\mathbb P(S_N>M)\le C/M$. Since the events increase to $\{S:=\sum_\alpha(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\xi_\alpha^2>M\}$, countable additivity gives $\mathbb P(S>M)\le C/M$; letting integer $M\to\infty$ shows $S<\infty$ on a common event $\Omega_0$ of probability one. [F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $f\in\mathcal S_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$ put $c_\alpha(f)=\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle$. On $\Omega_0$, [F11] and [F3] give $\sum_\alpha|\xi_\alpha c_\alpha(f)|\le S^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_\alpha(1+|\alpha|)^4|c_\alpha(f)|^2\bigr)^{1/2}<\infty$. Thus $W_0(f):=\sum_\alpha\xi_\alpha c_\alpha(f)$ converges absolutely for every $f$ on the same event, is real-linear, and satisfies $|W_0(f)|\le S^{1/2}\|H^2f\|_2$. The last quantity is a continuous Schwartz seminorm by [F3], so each sample is a tempered distribution. Set $W_0=0$ outside $\Omega_0$. Every evaluation $W_0(f)$ is measurable as the almost-sure limit of measurable finite sums, hence $W_0$ is measurable for the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra. [A2, F2, F3, F11, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The partial sums for $W_0(f)$ converge in $L^2(\Omega,\mathbb P)$ as well: independence, unit variance, and Parseval in [F10] make their squared $L^2$ tail equal to the corresponding tail of $\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha(f)|^2=\|f\|_2^2$. For any finite real combination $\sum_j t_jW_0(f_j)$, a finite partial sum is a linear combination of independent standard normals, with characteristic function $\prod_\alpha e^{-t^2c_\alpha^2/2}=e^{-t^2\sum_\alpha c_\alpha^2/2}$; by [F10] its variance converges to $\|\sum_jt_jf_j\|_2^2$. If $X_N\to X$ in $L^2$, then $|\mathbb E e^{itX_N}-\mathbb E e^{itX}|\le|t|\,\mathbb E|X_N-X|\le|t|\|X_N-X\|_2\to0$, so the limit has the centered normal characteristic function with that variance. Hence the family is jointly Gaussian, centered, and $\mathbb E[W_0(f)W_0(g)]=\int f(x)g(x)\,d^2x$. [F2, F10, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Set $\Phi(f)=W_0(T_mf)$. Each sample in $\Omega_0$ is a continuous real-linear functional of $f$ because both $W_0$ and $T_m$ are continuous on Schwartz space; outside $\Omega_0$ it is zero. Thus $\Phi$ is a measurable $\mathcal S'_\mathbb R$-valued random variable for the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra. From step 4.1 its covariance is $\mathbb E[\Phi(f)\Phi(g)]=\int T_mf(x)T_mg(x)\,d^2x$. Applying [F9] and changing variables $p=2\pi\xi$ gives $(2\pi)^{-2}\int\widehat{T_mf}(p)\overline{\widehat{T_mg}(p)}\,d^2p$. Since $f,g$ are real, $\widehat f(-p)=\overline{\widehat f(p)}$ and $\widehat g(-p)=\overline{\widehat g(p)}$; the substitution $p\mapsto-p$ changes this to $(2\pi)^{-2}\int\overline{\widehat f(p)}\widehat g(p)w_m(p)^2\,d^2p=C_m(f,g)$ by step 1.2. The finite-dimensional distributions remain centered Gaussian by step 4.1 and linearity of $T_m$. [F7, F9, step 4.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** [A1] and the hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 In $\mathfrak l_{\mathbb C}$ set $L_i=(J_i+iK_i)/2$ and $R_i=(J_i-iK_i)/2$. Expanding the stated brackets gives $[L_i,L_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$, $[R_i,R_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}R_k$, and $[L_i,R_j]=0$. The real span $\mathfrak k=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{L_i,R_i\}$ has compact Lie-algebra bracket: with $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, the basis $-i\sigma_i/2$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ has the same $\epsilon_{ijk}$ brackets. The two summands commute, and $\mathfrak k\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C=\mathfrak l_{\mathbb C}$ because $J_i=L_i+R_i$ and $K_i=(L_i-R_i)/i$. [given, A1, algebra]

1.2 Let $G=\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{SU}(2)$, whose Lie algebra is $\mathfrak k$. The matrices $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-\overline b&\overline a\end{pmatrix}$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$ identify $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ with the unit quaternions and hence with $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$, so $G$ is compact. To prove simple connectivity in the form needed here, take any piecewise-smooth based loop in $S^3$. Uniform continuity gives a finite subdivision on which each subarc lies in an open hemisphere. If $\delta(t)$ is the short great-circle arc between its endpoints, then $H(s,t)=((1-s)\gamma(t)+s\delta(t))/\|(1-s)\gamma(t)+s\delta(t)\|$ is defined throughout that hemisphere, fixes the endpoints, and homotopes the subarc to $\delta$. Each great-circle arc lies in the intersection of $S^3$ with a proper two-dimensional linear subspace $P_j\subset\mathbb R^4$. A finite union of proper linear subspaces cannot cover $\mathbb R^4$: induct on their number; after choosing $x$ outside $P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1}$, if $x\notin P_n$ we are done, and otherwise choose $y\notin P_n$; the line $x+ty$ meets each $P_j$ in at most one parameter value, so a real $t$ outside the finite forbidden set gives a point outside all $P_j$. Thus the resulting polygonal loop omits some $q\in S^3$. Stereographic projection identifies $S^3\setminus\{q\}$ with $\mathbb R^3$; straight-line contraction there to the basepoint fixes the loop endpoints and is piecewise smooth. Hence every piecewise-smooth based loop contracts through piecewise-smooth based loops. Applying this factorwise proves the required property for $G$. [F2, given, construct]

2.1 Complexify $\rho$ and $c$ and, on $W=V\oplus\mathbb C$, define $\widetilde\rho(X)(v,z)=(\rho(X)v+zc(X),0)$ for $X\in\mathfrak k$. The representation identity for $\rho$ and the cocycle identity for $c$ give $[\widetilde\rho(X),\widetilde\rho(Y)](v,z)=([\rho(X),\rho(Y)]v+z(\rho(X)c(Y)-\rho(Y)c(X)),0)=\widetilde\rho([X,Y])(v,z)$, so $\widetilde\rho$ is a finite-dimensional Lie-algebra representation. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Reparameterize each smooth path segment to $[0,1]$. For a piecewise-smooth path $\gamma$ put $a(t)=\gamma(t)^{-1}\dot\gamma(t)\in\mathfrak k$ and $A(t)=\widetilde\rho(a(t))$. Solve $U'=UA$, $U(0)=I$, separately on each segment and concatenate. On a segment with $\|A\|\le M$, the Picard series has $n$th term $\int_{0\le t_1\le\cdots\le t_n\le t}A(t_1)\cdots A(t_n)\,dt_1\cdots dt_n$, bounded by $M^n/n!$; it converges uniformly and termwise integration verifies the integral equation. If $D$ is the difference of two solutions with $D(0)=0$, then $\|D(t)\|\le M\int_0^t\|D(r)\|dr$; iterating gives $\|D(t)\|\le\sup\|D\|M^nt^n/n!\to0$, proving uniqueness. Solving $V'=-AV$, $V(0)=I$, by the same series gives $(UV)'=0$ and $UV=I$, so each transport matrix is invertible. Concatenating paths multiplies their transports in order, since on the second segment the solution with initial value $U_1$ is $U_1$ times the solution with initial value $I$. For a piecewise-smooth endpoint-fixed homotopy $\Gamma(s,t)$, the series terms and their $s$-derivatives are uniformly bounded by $M^n/n!$ and $nLM^{n-1}/n!$, respectively, where $L=\sup\|\partial_sA\|$ and we enlarge $M$ so $M\ge1$. Both series converge uniformly; integrating the derivative series in $s$ shows the limit $U$ is differentiable in $s$. Put $a=\Gamma^{-1}\partial_t\Gamma$ and $b=\Gamma^{-1}\partial_s\Gamma$. Direct differentiation yields $\partial_sa-\partial_tb=[a,b]$. The matrix-valued form $\theta=g^{-1}dg$ satisfies $d\theta=-\theta\wedge\theta$, by differentiating $g^{-1}g=I$; equivalently $d\theta+\frac12[\theta,\theta]=0$. Applying the representation from step 2.1 gives $A_s-B_t=[A,B]$, where $B=\widetilde\rho(b)$. For $K=U_s-UB$, differentiation now gives $K_t=KA+U(BA+A_s-AB-B_t)=KA$, and $K(s,0)=0$ because the initial endpoint is fixed. The uniqueness just proved gives $K=0$; at the fixed terminal endpoint $B(s,1)=0$, so $U_s(s,1)=0$. Thus transport is invariant under these homotopies. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ run from $e$ to the same $g$, the loop $\gamma_1$ followed by the reverse of $\gamma_2$ contracts by step 1.2, so its transport is $I$; the analogous loop using $\gamma_2$ shows the two transports agree. Hence transport is path-independent. Locally near $g_0$, choose paths from $e$ to $g_0^{-1}g$ varying smoothly with $g$ in a coordinate ball; the same uniform-series bounds imply continuous dependence on $g$, so $U$ is continuous. Finally, left-translating a path from $e$ to $h$ and concatenating it after a path from $e$ to $g$ gives $U(gh)=U(g)U(h)$, since left translation preserves $\gamma^{-1}\dot\gamma$. Thus $U$ is a continuous group representation. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The block form of $\widetilde\rho$ makes $U(g)=\begin{pmatrix}R(g)&b(g)\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, and its group law gives $b(hg)=R(h)b(g)+b(h)$. Identify each $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ with the unit quaternions and regard $S^3$ as the unit quaternions. For an explicit normalized round-volume integral, let $\chi(t)=0$ for $t\le1/3$ and $\chi(t)=e^{-1/(t-1/3)}$ for $t>1/3$. For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_4)\in S^3$, put $D(x)=\sum_{j=1}^4(\chi(x_j)+\chi(-x_j))$ and $\psi_{j,\pm}(x)=\chi(\pm x_j)/D(x)$. Since some $|x_j|\ge1/2$, $D(x)>0$; these eight smooth nonnegative functions sum to $1$ and have supports compactly contained in $U_{j,\pm}=\{\pm x_j>1/4\}$. In the chart given by the other three coordinates $y$, the sphere is $x_j=\pm\sqrt{1-|y|^2}$, the metric matrix is $G=I+yy^{\mathsf T}/(1-|y|^2)$, and therefore $\sqrt{\det G}=(1-|y|^2)^{-1/2}$. Define $I(f)=\sum_{j,\pm}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\psi_{j,\pm}(x(y))f(x(y))(1-|y|^2)^{-1/2}\,dy$, extending each integrand by zero outside its chart. Each term is continuous with compact support inside the chart, so [F1]–[F2] make it a finite Riemann integral. Its sum $I(1)$ is finite and positive: at $x=(1,0,0,0)$ one partition function is positive on a neighborhood, and on a small coordinate cube there the integrand has a positive lower bound. Set $\nu(f)=I(f)/I(1)$. This is the normalized round-volume functional. Its chart definition is independent of a finite subordinate chart partition: insert the second partition into each summand; each product has compact support in the chart overlap, and the metric identity $G(x)=DT(x)^{\mathsf T}G(Tx)DT(x)$ gives $\sqrt{\det G(x)}=|\det DT(x)|\sqrt{\det G(Tx)}$. Then [F3] transfers each compactly supported integral, and summing the finite terms gives equality. Quaternion left multiplication is an orthogonal map of $\mathbb R^4$, hence an isometry of this metric; using the transported charts and partition in the same identity gives $\nu(f\circ L_q)=\nu(f)$. The functional is positive and normalized, so its integral triangle inequality gives $|\nu(h)|\le\sup|h|$. Define the product round-volume functional on continuous $F:G\to\mathbb C$ by $\mu(F)=\nu(q\mapsto\nu(r\mapsto F(q,r)))$. The inner function is continuous because $F$ is uniformly continuous on compact $S^3\times S^3$ and the displayed norm bound holds. The product functional is normalized and left invariant by applying the factor identity twice. Since $b$ is continuous on compact $G$ and $V$ is finite-dimensional, $\bar v:=\mu(b)$ exists coordinatewise. Left invariance and the cocycle formula give $R(h)\bar v+b(h)=\mu(g\mapsto b(hg))=\bar v$ for every $h\in G$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Differentiate the fixed-point identity of step 4.1 at $h=\exp(tX)$ and $t=0$. The path equation defining $U$ gives $dR_e(X)=\rho(X)$ and $db_e(X)=c(X)$: these are the upper-left and upper-right blocks of $\widetilde\rho(X)$ in step 2.1. Hence $\rho(X)\bar v+c(X)=0$ for $X\in\mathfrak k$. Set $v=-\bar v$. The identity $c(X)=\rho(X)v$ extends complex-linearly from $\mathfrak k$ to $\mathfrak l_{\mathbb C}$ by step 1.1, and hence holds for every original $X\in\mathfrak l$. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** [A1], [F1], and the false assertion in the Statement.

1.1 On $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with standard basis $(e_n)_{n\ge1}$ define $D(A)=\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2|x_n|^2<\infty\}$ and $(Ax)_n=nx_n$. Finite sequences lie in $D(A)$ and are dense. For $x\in D(A)$, $\langle Ax,x\rangle=\sum n|x_n|^2\ge0$ and the sum converges by Cauchy–Schwarz, so $A$ is nonnegative. [given, algebra]

2.1 The operator is self-adjoint. If $y\in D(A^*)$, there is $z\in\ell^2$ with $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every finite sequence $x$; choosing $x=e_n$ gives $z_n=ny_n$, so $\sum n^2|y_n|^2=\|z\|^2<\infty$ and $y\in D(A)$. Conversely, if $y\in D(A)$ then $z=(ny_n)\in\ell^2$ satisfies the adjoint identity for every $x\in D(A)$ by convergence of the inner products. Thus $D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $A^*=A$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The inverse of $I+A$ is the bounded diagonal operator $B e_n=(n+1)^{-1}e_n$. Indeed for any $x\in\ell^2$, $y_n=x_n/(n+1)$ satisfies $\sum n^2|y_n|^2\le\sum|x_n|^2$, and $(I+A)y=x$. The operator $B$ is positive and injective. The vector $y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}$ belongs to $\ell^2$ but not to $\operatorname{Ran}B$, since $Bx=y$ would require $x_n=(n+1)/n$, which is not square-summable. Hence $B$ is not surjective and $0\in\sigma(B)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Define $E_B(S)x=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}x_ne_n$ for Borel $S\subseteq\sigma(B)$. Each value is an orthogonal coordinate projection and $E_B(\sigma(B))=I$. For disjoint Borel $S_k$, each coordinate $n$ occurs in at most one projection, so the partial sums $\sum_{k\le N}E_B(S_k)x$ converge in $\ell^2$ to $E_B(\bigcup_kS_k)x$: the squared norm of the omitted coordinates is a tail of the convergent nonnegative series $\sum_n|x_n|^2$. Thus $E_B$ is strongly countably additive. It integrates the coordinate function to $B$, because its integral acts diagonally by $(n+1)^{-1}$ on each $e_n$. For every $x$, the scalar measure $\langle E_B(\cdot)x,x\rangle=\sum_n|x_n|^2\delta_{(n+1)^{-1}}$ is regular: after retaining the first $N$ atoms its remaining mass is $\sum_{n>N}|x_n|^2\to0$, while the finite atomic measure is regular. Hence [F1] identifies this regular PVM with the bounded-resolvent spectral PVM. Since no atom is at zero, $E_B(\{0\})=0$, although step 3.1 proves $0\in\sigma(B)$. This refutes the asserted implication and shows why a zero spectral projection must be distinguished from a spectral value. [A1, F1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Fix a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a finite index set $A$ with real basis $\{t^a\}_{a\in A}$, and a finite species index set $I$. Let $\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}:=\mathfrak g\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ be the complexification of [[def-complexification-of-a-real-lie-algebra]], with complex scalar multiplication on the second tensor factor and the complex-bilinear bracket specified on pure tensors by $[X\otimes z,Y\otimes w]=[X,Y]\otimes zw$ for $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C$. Identify $X\in\mathfrak g$ with its canonical real embedding $X\otimes1$; in particular $t^a$ in a representation argument means $t^a\otimes1$. For each $i\in I$, let $V_i$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $\rho_i:\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_i)$ be a complex-linear Lie-algebra representation, so $\rho_i([U,V])=\rho_i(U)\rho_i(V)-\rho_i(V)\rho_i(U)$. Attach the bookkeeping label $\chi_i=L$ to each species. In this interface, a “left-handed Weyl species” means exactly the data $(V_i,\rho_i,\chi_i=L)$; the label is not a spinor field or a chirality operator. No spacetime manifold, spinor bundle or field, kinetic operator or action, integration of $\rho_i$ to a gauge group, regulator, effective action, or gauge-variation map is constructed or assumed.

Set $T^a_{R_i}:=\rho_i(t^a)$ and define $\{A,B\}:=AB+BA$ for endomorphisms of $V_i$. The algebraic cubic representation coefficient is
$$d^{abc}=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}\!\left(T^a_{R_i}\{T^b_{R_i},T^c_{R_i}\}\right)\in\mathbb C.$$
The basis and generator normalization are fixed as part of the data. No factor $1/2$ is included in the anticommutator. If $T^{(b}T^{c)}=(T^bT^c+T^cT^b)/2$, then $d^{abc}$ is twice $\sum_i\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}(T^a_{R_i}T^{(b}_{R_i}T^{c)}_{R_i})$. strategy.before:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Proof technique:** direct Gaussian density and translation.

**Given:** The objects and conventions in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1]–[F2], $\gamma_{K^{-1}}$ has Lebesgue density $c_K\exp(-\tfrac12x^TKx)$, where $c_K=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(K^{-1})^{-1/2}>0$. The expectation in the Statement is therefore the ratio of the displayed Lebesgue integrals, provided the numerator is finite. [A1, F1, F2, given]

1.2 Since $K$ is invertible, direct expansion gives
$$\tfrac12x^TKx-j^Tx=\tfrac12(x-K^{-1}j)^TK(x-K^{-1}j)-\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j.$$
The translation $x\mapsto x-K^{-1}j$ preserves Lebesgue measure by [F3]–[F5], so the numerator is the denominator multiplied by $\exp(\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j)$. The denominator is finite and positive because it is the normalizing integral of the probability density in [F2]; hence the numerator is also finite, and division proves both equalities. Expanding the same square proves the action identity. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Proof technique:** direct spectral calculus with a finite-regulator Gaussian identity.

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Definition.

1.1 The actual proof of [F1] uses Cauchy–Schwarz for its resolvent lower bound and closedness of $A$ for its resolvent graph argument. [F2] supplies the former. By [A1]–[A2] countable choice is available, so [F3] applies and self-adjointness gives $A=A^*$, hence $A$ is closed. This records the actual inputs of [F1]'s proof; the carrier's complete conditional proof was inspected. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Let $g_M(a)=(M^2+a)^{-1}$. By [F1], $g_M(A)$ is bounded with norm at most $M^{-2}$. Moreover, $\int a^2g_M(a)^2\,d\langle E_A(a)u,u\rangle\le\|u\|^2$ for every $u\in H$, so the domain formula for $A$ puts $g_M(A)u$ in $D(A)$. For any $u\in H$, truncate the spectral integrals to $[0,n]$; on each truncation the bounded Borel calculus is multiplicative, and the domain criterion just verified gives the graph limit $A g_M(A)u=\int a g_M(a)\,dE_A(a)u$. Hence $(M^2I+A)g_M(A)u=\int(M^2+a)g_M(a)\,dE_A(a)u=u$. For $v\in D(A)$, the same truncation and scalar multiplication give $g_M(A)(M^2I+A)v=\int g_M(a)(M^2+a)\,dE_A(a)v=v$. Thus $K^{-1}=g_M(A)$ and $\|K^{-1}\|\le M^{-2}$. Finally, the positive scalar multiplier gives $\langle J,K^{-1}J\rangle=\int g_M(a)\,d\langle E_A(a)J,J\rangle\ge0$, so the quadratic form is real. [A3, A4, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 In a finite real regulator with symmetric positive-definite matrix $K$, [F4] gives the normalized source integral $\exp(\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j)$. Taking its negative logarithm using [F5] gives the effective-action shift $-\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j$. No determinant or Lebesgue integral beyond that finite regulator enters the definition. [F4, F5, given, algebra] ∎

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Proof technique:** direct scalar remainder and the spectral functional calculus.

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 For every $a\ge0$, putting $x=a/M^2$ and multiplying by $1+x$ gives
$$\frac1{M^2+a}=M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-a/M^2)^r+
M^{-2}\frac{(-a/M^2)^{N+1}}{1+a/M^2}.$$
This finite geometric identity also holds at $a=0$ and for $N=0$. [given, algebra]

1.2 On $J=P_EJ$, the spectral variable satisfies $0\le a\le E^2$. Therefore every polynomial term $A^rJ$ is defined, and the remainder multiplier satisfies
$$\left|M^{-2}\frac{(-a/M^2)^{N+1}}{1+a/M^2}\right|
\le M^{-2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1},$$
because $1+a/M^2\ge1$. Extend this bounded multiplier by zero outside $[0,E^2]$ and apply [F1]. With [F2] this identifies the inverse kernel and proves the vector identity defining $R_NJ$ and its norm bound. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the action remainder equals $\tfrac12|\langle J,R_NJ\rangle|$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F3] and step 1.2 give the claimed bound. The factor $(E^2/M^2)^{N+1}$ decreases to zero only when $E<M$; for $E\ge M$ the same finite-order bound remains true but need not be small. [F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Proof technique:** direct measurability and positivity check.

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Definition.

1.1 The map $(x,z)\mapsto f(x+z)$ is Borel because addition is continuous and $f$ is Borel. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is sigma-finite because $\mathbb R^d=\bigcup_{n\ge1}[-n,n]^d$ and each cube has finite measure; $\gamma_C$ is a probability by [F1]. Thus [F2] makes $x\mapsto T_Cf(x)$ Borel, including when the integral is infinite. [A1, F1, F2, given]

1.2 For finite nonnegative Borel $V$, $g_x(z):=e^{-V(x+z)}$ is Borel and satisfies $0<g_x(z)\le1$. Its integral against the probability $\gamma_C$ is at most one. It is strictly positive: if the integral were zero, each set $\{z:g_x(z)\ge1/n\}$ would have measure zero, while their countable union is all of $\mathbb R^d$, contradicting $\gamma_C(\mathbb R^d)=1$. Thus $T_C(e^{-V})(x)\in(0,1]$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], the logarithm is defined at these values. Its continuity follows directly from [F4]: for $y_0>0$ and $\epsilon>0$, strict increase and continuity of $\exp$ give $\exp(\log y_0-\epsilon)<y_0<\exp(\log y_0+\epsilon)$; put $\delta=\min\{y_0-\exp(\log y_0-\epsilon),\exp(\log y_0+\epsilon)-y_0\}>0$. If $y>0$ and $|y-y_0|<\delta$, then $\exp(\log y_0-\epsilon)<y<\exp(\log y_0+\epsilon)$, and strict monotonicity gives $|\log y-\log y_0|<\epsilon$. Hence $V_C$ is finite, nonnegative, and Borel. If $C=0$, then for each coordinate $Z_i$, $\mathbb E Z_i^2=C_{ii}=0$. For every $n\ge1$, $0=\mathbb E Z_i^2\ge n^{-2}\mathbb P(|Z_i|\ge n^{-1})$, so $Z_i=0$ almost surely; the finite intersection gives $Z=0$ almost surely and $\gamma_0=\delta_0$; hence $T_0f=f$ and $V_0=V$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Proof technique:** product Gaussian law and Tonelli.

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the Statement.

1.1 On $(\mathbb R^d,\gamma_{C_1})\times(\mathbb R^d,\gamma_{C_2})$, the sum map $(y,z)\mapsto y+z$ has characteristic function
$$
\int e^{iu\cdot(y+z)}\,d(\gamma_{C_1}\times\gamma_{C_2})
=\exp(-u^TC_1u/2)\exp(-u^TC_2u/2)
=\exp[-u^T(C_1+C_2)u/2].
$$
The product measure exists by [F3], the integrand is bounded and therefore integrable, and [F4] justifies the iterated integral/product factorization. Since $C_1+C_2$ is positive semidefinite, [F2] and [F5] identify the pushforward under addition as $\gamma_{C_1+C_2}$. This includes singular and zero covariances. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given]

2.1 The function $(x,y,z)\mapsto f(x+y+z)$ is nonnegative and Borel. Apply [F6] to integrate first in $y$ and then in $z$; the resulting iterated integral equals the integral against the product law of $(y,z)$. By step 1.1 its pushforward under addition is $\gamma_{C_1+C_2}$. Therefore
$$\int\left(\int f(x+z+y)\,d\gamma_{C_1}(y)\right)d\gamma_{C_2}(z)
=\int f(x+w)\,d\gamma_{C_1+C_2}(w),$$
including the value $+\infty$. By [F1] this is exactly $T_{C_2}(T_{C_1}f)(x)=T_{C_1+C_2}f(x)$. [F1, F6, step 1.1, given]

3.1 For finite nonnegative Borel $V$, [F1] gives $\exp[-V_{C_1}(x)]=T_{C_1}(e^{-V})(x)$ and the corresponding identity after applying $C_2$. Substituting $f=e^{-V}$ into step 2.1 proves the stated potential-weight identity. Since the normalized Gaussian integrals are expectations under probability laws, no determinant factor occurs. No differentiation or covariance-path limit was used. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Proof technique:** direct multiplier calculation and compactly supported unit vectors.

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 By [A1]–[A2], the AC and Countable Choice assumptions of [F2] and [F4] hold. Apply [F2] with $m(p)=p^2$ on the sigma-finite positive-measure space $(\mathbb R,dp)$; sigma-finiteness follows from $\mathbb R=\bigcup_{n\ge1}[-n,n]$ and $[-1,1]$ has positive finite measure. It gives the self-adjoint nonnegative multiplication operator $A$ with the displayed domain and spectral calculus. The multiplier $(M^2+p^2)^{-1}$ is bounded by $M^{-2}$ and maps $H$ into $D(A)$ because $p^2/(M^2+p^2)\le1$; pointwise multiplication then shows it is the two-sided inverse of $M^2I+A$. For $u$ with bounded support, every $A^ru$ is in $H$. Pointwise finite geometric division gives
$$
(M^2+p^2)^{-1}-M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-p^2/M^2)^r=r_N(p^2),
$$
so the remainder on such $u$ is multiplication by $r_N(p^2)$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 The target coefficient $C_N:=M^{-2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1}$ is finite and is strictly less than $M^{-2}$. If $N=0$, $|r_0(q)|=M^{-2}(q/M^2)/(1+q/M^2)\to M^{-2}>C_0$ as $q\to\infty$. If $N\ge1$, $|r_N(q)|=M^{-2}(q/M^2)^{N+1}/(1+q/M^2)\to\infty$. In either case choose $P>0$ so that $|r_N(p^2)|>C_N$ for every $p\in[P,P+M]$, and put $u=M^{-1/2}\mathbf1_{[P,P+M]}$. The interval has Lebesgue measure $M$, so $\|u\|_2^2=M^{-1}\int_P^{P+M}1\,dp=1$; its bounded support puts it in every $D(A^r)$, while
$$\|r_N(A)u\|_2^2=M^{-1}\int_P^{P+M}|r_N(p^2)|^2\,dp>C_N^2.$$
Thus the full-space bound fails. The restriction $E<M$ is precisely what makes the proposed low-energy coefficient smaller than the $N=0$ high-momentum limit; the example does not contradict the band-limited theorem. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

$e>0$ is the magnitude of the elementary charge, in C; and $\mu_0>0$ is the
vacuum permeability, in H m$^{-1}$, used here as a positive parameter without
assigning it a numerical value. Set
$$g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}>0,$$
which is dimensionless. These are the adopted QFT SI conventions.

Let $I$ be a finite, possibly empty, set of leg labels. For each $i\in I$,
choose an energy $E_i>0$ in J and a physical velocity
$\mathbf v_{i,\mathrm{phys}}\in\mathbb R^3$ in m s$^{-1}$ with
$|\mathbf v_{i,\mathrm{phys}}|<c$. Write
$v_i=\mathbf v_{i,\mathrm{phys}}/c\in\mathbb R^3$, so $v_i$ is
dimensionless and $|v_i|<1$. Also choose a dimensionless charge number
$Q_i\in\mathbb R$ (the assigned physical charge is $eQ_i$ in C) and an
orientation $\eta_i\in\{-1,1\}$, where $-1$ denotes an incoming leg and
$+1$ an outgoing leg. Assume charge balance
$\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i=0$. For four-vectors
$a=(a^0,\mathbf a),b=(b^0,\mathbf b)\in\mathbb R^4$, write
$h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$ and
$h(a,b)=a^0b^0-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$ for the algebraic contraction
with signature $(+,-,-,-)$ used in this model.

For $n\in S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and angular frequency
$\nu>0$ in s$^{-1}$, with associated model photon energy $\hbar\nu$ in J,
put $p_i=E_i(1,v_i)$ and $q=\hbar\nu(1,n)$ in $\mathbb R^4$. On
$$\mathscr Q=\{\hbar\nu(1,n):\nu>0,\ n\in S^2\}\subset\mathbb R^4,$$
define the prescribed current $J:\mathscr Q\to\mathbb R^4$ and angular
coefficient $K:S^2\to\mathbb R^4$ by
$$J(q)=\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i\frac{p_i}{h(p_i,q)},\qquad K(n)=\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i\frac{(1,v_i)}{1-v_i\cdot n}.$$
Because $|v_i\cdot n|\le |v_i|<1$, every denominator
$1-v_i\cdot n$ is strictly positive.
The data make $h(p_i,q)=E_i\hbar\nu(1-v_i\cdot n)>0$ and

eikonal current in the model. Here “prescribed eikonal current” means exactly

scattering-amplitude factorization or approximation is asserted.

$d\Omega$ denotes its Euclidean chart surface measure: for a finite regular
injective $C^1$ chart cover $X_j:V_j\to S^2$, where each $V_j$ is open in
$\mathbb R^2$, with $C^1$ coordinate
transitions and a subordinate ambient partition of unity $\chi_j$ whose supports are compactly
contained in the chart neighborhoods, its integral on a nonnegative Borel
function $F$ is
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\Omega=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_jF)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy.$$
This is the chart-independent induced surface integral. Write
$K(n)=(K^0(n),\mathbf K(n))$ and define
$K_\perp(n)=(I_3-nn^T)\mathbf K(n)$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$
identity matrix. Put
$$b_0(n)=\frac{gK_\perp(n)}{\sqrt{2(2\pi)^3}},\qquad b(n)=\mathbf1_A(n)b_0(n),\qquad C=\int_{S^2}|b(n)|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$

for these finite balanced subluminal legs; since $A$ is Borel,
$b\in L^2$ and $0\le C\le\int_{S^2}|b_0|^2d\Omega<\infty$.

where the second dot product is the complex-bilinear extension. The fiber
Hermitian pairing is $\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline{a_j}b_j$, with
norm $|a|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$. Set
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$

second-variable-linear. For $\mathbf k\ne0$,

and $P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\widehat{\mathbf k}\widehat{\mathbf k}^{T}$, the
Euclidean orthogonal projection onto the fiber plane perpendicular to
$\mathbf k$; assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$. Its multiplier is an
orthogonal projection on $\mathcal H$, so its range is closed. The transverse
one-particle Hilbert space
is
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}=\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for a.e. }\mathbf k\ne0\},$$

product is extended complex-bilinearly in the transverse condition. This is
the transverse one-particle space used in this model.

$\mathcal H_T^{\widehat\otimes m}$, with product pairing on elementary
tensors. Here $S_m$ is the permutation group and
$U_\pi(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_m)=

$$P_{s,m}=\frac1{m!}\sum_{\pi\in S_m}U_\pi,\qquad \mathcal H_s^{(m)}=\operatorname{Ran}P_{s,m};$$

symmetric bosonic Fock space is

$\epsilon:\mathcal H_T\to\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ by
$$\epsilon(f)=\bigoplus_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{P_{s,m}(f^{\otimes m})}{\sqrt{m!}}.$$

$P_{s,m}(f^{\otimes m})=f^{\otimes m}$ for $m\ge1$; write this tensor as
$f^{\otimes_s m}$.

$\nu(\mathbf k)=c|\mathbf k|$ in s$^{-1}$, with $\mathbf k$ in m$^{-1}$.

$\hbar\nu(\mathbf k)=\hbar c|\mathbf k|$ in J. Define its normalized
coherent vector by
$$\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}\|^2}{2}\right)\epsilon(f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}).$$

$B_1,\ldots,B_r$ of $(\varepsilon,\Lambda)$ into disjoint Borel intervals,

$H_j=\{u\in\mathcal H_T:u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ a.e. unless }\nu(\mathbf k)\in B_j\}$.

disjoint.

$$P_{s,M}\left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^r\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^{m_j}u_{j,\ell}\right),\qquad u_{j,\ell}\in H_j,$$

threshold frequency is assigned to the resolved band; its exact assignment
does not change any $L^2$ vector or probability because a single frequency
has zero one-particle measure.

detector response or an interacting QED scattering law.

$$
d\Gamma(J_{\mathbf a})=\sum_{r=1}^{n} I^{\otimes(r-1)}\otimes J_{\mathbf a}\otimes I^{\otimes(n-r)}.
$$
In this statement $d\Gamma(J_{\mathbf a})$ denotes that Stone generator; the formula specifies its action on the stated finite-particle domain.

Let $\mathscr D_{\rm fin}(\mathcal D)$ be the vacuum plus the finite linear span of symmetrized elementary tensors whose one-particle factors lie in $\mathcal D$. It is a dense invariant domain, and on it the Fock total generators satisfy $[J_i^{\mathrm F},J_j^{\mathrm F}]=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}J_k^{\mathrm F}$.

For helicity $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$, define $N_\sigma$ on the $n$-particle sector by

strategy.before:
1.1 Every class in $A$ is uniquely $a+bx$ with $a,b\in\mathbb C$, and $(a+bx)(c+dx)=ac+(ad+bc)x$ because $x^2=0$. This is the quotient of the associative commutative algebra $\mathbb C[x]$, so $A$ is a two-dimensional commutative unital associative algebra with nonzero nilpotent $x$. [given, algebra]

1.2 The pairing values are $b(1,1)=0$, $b(1,x)=1$, $b(x,1)=1$, and $b(x,x)=0$, so its matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and determinant $-1\ne0$. Hence $b$ is nondegenerate. [given, algebra]

2.1 Define $\Delta(1)=1\otimes x+x\otimes1$ and $\Delta(x)=x\otimes x$. On both basis elements, $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta=\operatorname{id}_A$ as counit identities; the two coassociative composites on $1$ both equal $1\otimes x\otimes x+x\otimes1\otimes x+x\otimes x\otimes1$, and on $x$ both equal $x\otimes x\otimes x$. For the two Frobenius identities, bilinearity reduces to the four basis pairs $(1,1),(1,x),(x,1),(x,x)$; on these pairs all three composites $\Delta\mu$, $(1\otimes\mu)(\Delta\otimes1)$, and $(\mu\otimes1)(1\otimes\Delta)$ respectively equal $\Delta(1),\Delta(x),\Delta(x),0$. Thus the specified maps make $A$ a commutative Frobenius algebra. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 The ideal $(x)$ is maximal because $A/(x)\cong\mathbb C$. For every maximal ideal $M$, the quotient $A/M$ is a field and the image of $x$ there is nilpotent because $x^2=0$; a field has no nonzero nilpotents, so $x\in M$. Hence $0\ne x\in J(A)$, the intersection of all maximal left ideals, and $A$ is not semisimple under the stated definition. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 For $a=a_0+a_1x$ and $b=b_0+b_1x$, $h(a,b)=\overline{a_0}b_1+\overline{a_1}b_0$, so $h(a,b)=\overline{h(b,a)}$ and the form is Hermitian. Also $h(1+x,1+x)=\epsilon((1+x)^2)=2$ while $h(1-x,1-x)=\epsilon((1-x)^2)=-2$, so it takes both signs and is not positive definite. [given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1 the algebra is finite-dimensional, commutative, and Frobenius, so [F1] applies over $k=\mathbb C$ and gives the closed oriented two-dimensional TQFT. This conclusion uses the closed category only and adds no open/closed or positivity claim. [given, F1, step 2.1] ∎

Assume full AC and its inherited countable-choice consequences. Let $\mathcal C$ be a complex modular ribbon fusion category with finite simple-label set $I$, unit label $0$, simple pivotal dimensions $d_i$, twists $\theta_i$, and Hopf-link matrix $s$. Choose a square root $D\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ of $\sum_{i\in I}d_i^2$ and set $S=s/D$, $p_+=\sum_{i\in I}\theta_i d_i^2$, and $\kappa=p_+/D$. Modularity means that $s$ is invertible; no positivity of $d_i$ or $D$ is assumed.

$$|\mathcal C|:=\sum_{[c]\in\pi_0(\mathcal C)}\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(c)|}.$$

Let $K$ be a finite connected CW complex and $G$ a finite group. Choose an orientation of each 1-cell and, for each 2-cell, its based attaching word in the finite edge presentation of $\pi_1(K)$; the choice of base paths is part of that presentation. A **flat edge assignment** is a label $g_e\in G$ for every oriented 1-cell with $g_{\bar e}=g_e^{-1}$, such that each attaching word has holonomy $1$. If a word traverses edges $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ in that order with exponents $\epsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}$, its holonomy is $g_{e_m}^{\epsilon_m}\cdots g_{e_1}^{\epsilon_1}$.

Write $\operatorname{Flat}(K,G)$ for the finite set of flat assignments and $K_0$ for the vertices. The finite vertex gauge group $G^{K_0}$ acts by

$$(h\cdot g)_e=h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1},$$

where $s(e)$ and $t(e)$ are the source and target vertices. The **finite flat connection groupoid** $\mathcal C_G(K)$ is the action groupoid $\operatorname{Flat}(K,G)//G^{K_0}$: its objects are flat assignments and its arrows $g\to g'$ are the $h\in G^{K_0}$ with $h\cdot g=g'$. Its untwisted finite BF partition function is the groupoid cardinality

$$Z_G(K):=|\mathcal C_G(K)|=\sum_{[g]\in\operatorname{Flat}(K,G)/G^{K_0}}\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Stab}(g)|} =\frac{|\operatorname{Flat}(K,G)|}{|G|^{|K_0|}}.$$

This is a finite combinatorial model; it has no continuous Lie-algebra-valued connection integral or additional cocycle phase.

For a finite disconnected CW complex, define $\mathcal C_G(K)$ to be the product of the groupoids of its connected components; for the empty complex use the terminal groupoid.

statement.proposed:
Work in one named laboratory chart with spatial coordinate space $\mathbb R^3$ and time coordinate $t\in\mathbb R$. Let $q\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ be the framework charge parameter, let $m>0$ be an externally supplied mass parameter, and take the SI constants $c>0$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$ of the electromagnetic framework. Define the positive time constant

$$\tau:=\frac{q^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0mc^3}>0.$$

The units are $[q]=\mathrm C$, $[m]=\mathrm{kg}$, $[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $[\varepsilon_0]=\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, so $[\tau]=\mathrm s$. A prescribed external force is a continuous map $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with units $\mathrm N$. A particle trajectory in this model is a map $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with three continuous time derivatives; its velocity and acceleration are $v(t):=\dot x(t)$ and $a(t):=\ddot x(t)$, with units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The term point particle means that the model assigns one position $x(t)$ and no spatial extent.

Adopt, as an additional effective model postulate, the equation

$$m\bigl(a(t)-\tau\dot a(t)\bigr)=f(t)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

Both $ma$ and $m\tau\dot a$ have units of force. The dot on $a$ means differentiation with respect to the laboratory time. This equation is not obtained by evaluating the particle's singular Maxwell self-field in the adopted Lorentz force law. The previously developed prescribed-source radiation model does not define that self-interaction; this postulate introduces a separate effective equation.

For physical use on a compact interval $I\subset\mathbb R$, assume $f$ is continuously differentiable there, choose dimensionless tolerances $\eta,\delta\in(0,1)$ and a positive force scale $F_*$ with units $\mathrm N$, and state the chosen values. In this item, low-speed at tolerance $\eta$ means $\sup_{t\in I}|v(t)|\le\eta c$, and slowly varying relative to $\tau$ at tolerance $\delta$ means $\tau\sup_{t\in I}|\dot f(t)|\le\delta F_*$. These are explicit regime conventions for an application, not universal empirical thresholds. The ODE is an exact adopted equation on its mathematical domain; its physical interpretation is restricted to applications that state their regime and tolerances.

statement.proposed:
Use the equation and constants of the preceding postulate, with $m,\tau>0$. Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and continuous, and let a solution mean a continuously differentiable map $a:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $m(a-\tau\dot a)=f$ at every real time. Bounded for a vector map means each of its three real coordinates is bounded; in $\mathbb R^3$ this is equivalent to bounded Euclidean norm. The vector improper Riemann integral below is taken componentwise, with $\int_t^\infty h(s)\,ds:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_t^R h(s)\,ds$ when that limit exists. Then the integral converges absolutely, and

$$a_*(t):=\frac{1}{m\tau}\int_t^\infty \exp\!\left(-\frac{s-t}{\tau}\right)f(s)\,ds$$

is a bounded solution. For any fixed $t_0\in\mathbb R$, every solution has the form

$$a(t)=a_*(t)+C\exp\!\left(\frac{t-t_0}{\tau}\right),\qquad C\in\mathbb R^3$$

Here $C$ is a constant acceleration vector with units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

The only solution bounded on a future half-line $[T,\infty)$, for any finite $T$, is $a_*$. A nonzero $C$ gives an exponentially growing acceleration branch, called a runaway branch in this item. Moreover, there is a bounded smooth force that vanishes for $t\le0$, is nonzero for some $t\in(0,1)$, and for which $a_*(t)\ne0$ for every $t<0$. Preacceleration means this nonzero acceleration before the force begins; it is a property of the selected ODE branch, not an observation about a physical particle.

Assume the equation and bounded-force hypotheses of the preceding theorem: $m,\tau>0$, $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ is bounded and twice continuously differentiable, and the unique bounded-future solution $a_*$ is used. Suppose

$$M_2:=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|f''(t)|<\infty.$$

Since $f$ has units $\mathrm N$ and $t$ has units $\mathrm s$, $M_2$ has units $\mathrm{N\,s^{-2}}$.

Define the first-order reduction-of-order approximation by

$$a_{\mathrm{RO}}(t):=\frac{f(t)+\tau f'(t)}{m}.$$

Its residual when substituted into the adopted equation is exactly

$$m\bigl(a_{\mathrm{RO}}(t)-\tau a_{\mathrm{RO}}'(t)\bigr)-f(t)=-\tau^2 f''(t).$$

On the bounded-future branch the acceleration error obeys

$$|a_*(t)-a_{\mathrm{RO}}(t)|\le\frac{\tau^2 M_2}{m}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

The residual and bound are exact conditional statements about the prescribed-force ODE; they do not assert that a nonlinear self-consistent particle trajectory is approximated by $a_{\mathrm{RO}}$.

statement.proposed:
In the adopted equation, set $f=0$ and fix any $t_0\in\mathbb R$. For every constant acceleration vector $C\in\mathbb R^3$ with units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the acceleration $a_C(t)=C\exp((t-t_0)/\tau)$ is a solution. For any fixed position $x_0$ and velocity $v_0$ at $t_0$, a trajectory with that acceleration is

$$x_C(t)=x_0+v_0(t-t_0)+C\tau^2\left(\exp((t-t_0)/\tau)-1-\frac{t-t_0}{\tau}\right).$$

Thus the same position and velocity at $t_0$ admit different acceleration branches; $C\ne0$ grows exponentially as $t\to\infty$. This does not establish that any physical charge follows such a trajectory.

statement.proposed:
A phasor coefficient at frequency $\omega\in\mathbb R$ is a complex vector $g_0=g_R+ig_I\in\mathbb C^3$, with $g_R,g_I\in\mathbb R^3$, representing a real map $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by the real-part representation

$$g(t)=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(g_0\exp(-i\omega t)\right)=g_R\cos(\omega t)+g_I\sin(\omega t).$$

At $\omega=0$ this representation determines only $g_R$. Adopt the canonical static convention $g_0=G+i0$ for the constant function $g(t)\equiv G\in\mathbb R^3$; in particular the static force below has $v=0$ and $f_0=u+i0$. Static acceleration phasors use the same convention.

Let $\omega\in\mathbb R$ and $f_0=u+iv\in\mathbb C^3$, with $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$. For any $z=u+iv\in\mathbb C^3$, define $|z|:=\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^3|u_j|^2+\sum_{j=1}^3|v_j|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$, the Euclidean norm of its six real coordinates. The force amplitude $f_0$ has units N, $\omega$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and acceleration phasors have units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Prescribe the real force

$$f(t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(f_0\exp(-i\omega t)\right),$$

where real part is taken componentwise. The bounded-future acceleration has complex phasor amplitude

$$a_{*,0}=\frac{f_0}{m(1+i\omega\tau)}.$$

The first-order reduction-of-order acceleration $a_{\mathrm{RO}}=(f+\tau f')/m$ has phasor amplitude $a_{\mathrm{RO},0}=f_0(1-i\omega\tau)/m$. For $f_0\ne0$, the absolute amplitude error relative to the force acceleration scale $|f_0|/m$ is

$$\frac{|a_{*,0}-a_{\mathrm{RO},0}|}{|f_0|/m}=\frac{(\omega\tau)^2}{\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^2}}.$$

For any chosen tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, this relative amplitude error is at most $\epsilon$ exactly when

$$|\omega\tau|\le\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon^2+\sqrt{\epsilon^4+4\epsilon^2}}{2}}.$$

Hence small error at a small prescribed tolerance requires small $|\omega\tau|$; no universal numerical cutoff or experimental frequency response is asserted.

statement.proposed:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with the metric $d_1(q,r):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|q(a)-r(a)|$ and its induced topology, called the $\ell^1$ topology. This is a metric: symmetry, nonnegativity and separation follow coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows by summing $|q(a)-s(a)|\leq|q(a)-r(a)|+|r(a)-s(a)|$. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the probability measure on Borel subsets $B\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)$ that assigns mass
$$p_{n,\beta}\bigl(\{x^n\in\Omega_n:L_n(x^n)\in B\}\bigr).$$

For a real-valued function $f$ on a nonempty set $S$, define $\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\inf_{y\in S}f(y)\}$ and $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\sup_{y\in S}f(y)\}$; either set is empty if the corresponding extremum is not attained. For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $A\subseteq\Omega_n$ and an event $E\subseteq\Omega_n$ with $p^{\otimes n}(E)>0$, define the conditional probability by $p^{\otimes n}(A\mid E):=p^{\otimes n}(A\cap E)/p^{\otimes n}(E)$. For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $(K,d_K)$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $(\mu_n)_{n\geq1}$ be Borel probability measures on $K$. Let $I:K\to[0,+\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous, meaning that $\{x\in K:I(x)>a\}$ is open for every real $a$, and not identically $+\infty$. Assume the speed-$n$ large-deviation bounds
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(G)\geq-\inf_{x\in G}I(x)\quad\text{for every open }G\subseteq K,$$
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(C)\leq-\inf_{x\in C}I(x)\quad\text{for every closed }C\subseteq K,$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$. Let $F:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and put
$$Z_n:=\int_K e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x),\qquad c:=\sup_{x\in K}\bigl(F(x)-I(x)\bigr).$$
For Borel $B\subseteq K$, define the normalized exponential tilt
$$\nu_n^F(B):=Z_n^{-1}\int_B e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x).$$
Here a good rate function is a lower semicontinuous map $J:K\to[0,+\infty]$ whose sublevel sets $\{x:J(x)\leq a\}$ are compact for every real $a$. Then $Z_n$ is finite and positive,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln Z_n=c,$$
and $(\nu_n^F)$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with the good rate function $I_F(x):=I(x)-F(x)+c$. Its zero set is precisely $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in K}(F(x)-I(x)):=\{x\in K:F(x)-I(x)=c\}$, with $F(x)-(+\infty):=-\infty$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

This is a dimensionless mathematical model: $J$, $\beta$, $h$, and $\Phi_\beta$ are dimensionless, so $\beta J$ is dimensionless. The labels “coupling” and “inverse-temperature parameter” are conventional names here and do not assign physical units.

Let $\mathcal A=\{-1,+1\}$ with uniform reference law $p(\pm1)=1/2$. For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$ define its magnetization $m(q):=q(+1)-q(-1)\in[-1,1]$ and the mean-field energy density $h(q):=-Jm(q)^2/2$, where $J>0$. For inverse-temperature parameter $\beta\geq0$, the canonical macrostate variational objective from the finite-alphabet model is
$$\Phi_\beta(m):=\frac{1+m}{2}\ln(1+m)+\frac{1-m}{2}\ln(1-m)-\frac{\beta Jm^2}{2},\qquad -1\leq m\leq1,$$
where $0\ln0:=0$. This objective has the unique global minimizer $m=0$ when $\beta J\leq1$. When $\beta J>1$, its global minimizers are exactly $m=\pm m_\beta$, where $m_\beta\in(0,1)$ is the unique positive solution of
$$m=\tanh(\beta Jm),\qquad \tanh x:=\frac{\exp(2x)-1}{\exp(2x)+1}.$$

Take the binary alphabet $\mathcal A=\{1,0\}$ with uniform reference $p=(1/2,1/2)$ and continuous energy-density map $h(q)=q(1)^{1/4}$ on $\Delta(\mathcal A)$. With $H_2(x):=-x\ln x-(1-x)\ln(1-x)$ and $0\ln0:=0$, the constrained entropy from the finite-alphabet mean-field model is $s(u)=H_2(u^4)-\ln2$ for $0\leq u\leq1$. For $0<u\leq1/10$,
$$s''(u)=u^2\left[12\ln\frac{1-u^4}{u^4}-\frac{16}{1-u^4}\right]>0.$$
Each such energy lies in an interval of strict convexity and therefore has no affine upper supporting line of any slope. Consequently none of these microcanonical energies is realized by a canonical mean-field ensemble at any $\beta\in\mathbb R$.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, so $V$ is finite and $E$ is a set of two-element subsets of $V$. Fix an integer $Q\geq2$, write $[Q]=\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, and assign to each edge $e\in E$ a finite activity $v_e\in[0,\infty)$. A spin configuration is a function $\sigma:V\to[Q]$. Its unnormalized Potts weight and partition function are
$$w_P(\sigma):=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}\in E}\bigl(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}}\bigr),\qquad Z_P(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{\sigma:V\to[Q]}w_P(\sigma).$$
For $A\subseteq E$, let $G_A=(V,A)$, and let $k_G(A)$ be its number of connected components, counting isolated vertices; equivalently, these are the equivalence classes generated by the endpoint pairs of edges in $A$. Put $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. The unnormalized Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) weight and partition function are
$$w_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_G(A)}v_A,\qquad Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{FK}(A).$$
Both normalizers are finite and positive: the spin sum is finite with every term at least $1$, while the empty-edge FK term is $Q^{|V|}>0$. These are finite mathematical weights; no physical units or empirical status are assigned.

Use the Potts weight $w_P(\sigma)=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}}(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}})$ and FK weight $w_{FK}(A)=Q^{k_G(A)}\prod_{e\in A}v_e$ from the finite definitions. Define
$$W(\sigma,A):=\prod_{e\notin A}1\prod_{e\in A}v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}},\qquad (\sigma,A)\in[Q]^V\times2^E.$$
The normalized joint law $\nu(\sigma,A):=W(\sigma,A)/\sum_{\tau,B}W(\tau,B)$ has Potts marginal $w_P/Z_P$ and FK marginal $w_{FK}/Z_{FK}$, with $Z_P=Z_{FK}=\sum_{\tau,B}W(\tau,B)$. Conditional on an edge set $A$ of positive probability, the colors of its connected components are independent and uniform on $[Q]$. Thus for every $x,y\in V$,
$$\mathbb P(\sigma(x)=\sigma(y))=\frac1Q+\left(1-\frac1Q\right)\mathbb P_{FK}(x\leftrightarrow y),$$
where $x\leftrightarrow y$ means that $x$ and $y$ lie in the same component of $G_A$.

statement.proposed:
Input a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, integer $Q\geq2$, finite activities $v_e\in[0,\infty)$, a total edge order $e_1,\ldots,e_m$, and boundary data consisting of a set $B\subseteq V$ and an equivalence relation $\xi$ on $B$. The relation $\xi$ identifies prescribed boundary vertices before any edge is processed; its singleton classes give free boundary and its non-singleton classes give the wired classes. A vertex incident to no edge is isolated. Put $n_0:=|\{x\in V\setminus B:x\text{ is isolated}\}|$. At time $t$, the **active frontier** consists of the initially active boundary vertices $B$ together with vertices introduced at a processed edge, minus those already forgotten. A state is a set partition of the active frontier. Its blocks record equivalence generated by the initial boundary relation $\xi$ and processed present edges. A coefficient vector assigns a nonnegative real weight to each such partition.

Initialize the frontier as $B$ with partition $\xi$ and coefficient $Q^{n_0}$; if $B=\varnothing$, this is the empty partition. For $t=1,\ldots,m$, perform the following operations in order.

1. Introduce each endpoint of $e_t$ that is not yet active as a singleton block.
2. For each state $\pi$ of coefficient $c$, add $c$ to the same state (the edge is absent) and add $c v_{e_t}$ to $J_{uv}\pi$ (the edge is present), where $e_t=\{u,v\}$ and $J_{uv}\pi$ merges the blocks containing $u$ and $v$ and leaves all other blocks unchanged. If $u,v$ already share a block, $J_{uv}\pi=\pi$. Thus $J_{uv}^2=J_{uv}$ and the edge operator is $I+v_{e_t}J_{uv}$.
3. Forget vertices whose last incident edge is $e_t$. When removing a vertex empties its block, delete that block and multiply its coefficient by $Q$ once; otherwise just remove the vertex from its block. If several vertices in a block are forgotten at this step, the factor $Q$ is applied only when the last active member is removed.

After all edges are processed, forget any remaining active vertices by the same rule and return the coefficient of the empty partition. This includes boundary vertices with no incident edge; each surviving wired component is then counted once. Discrete $\xi$ gives free boundary, while non-singleton classes implement the stated wired boundary condition. A planar-strip annotation consists of a plane embedding, an ordered frontier list at every update, a noncrossing initial relation $\xi$, and the condition that every reachable connectivity partition is noncrossing. For an ordered frontier, “noncrossing” means that no two different blocks contain alternating points $a<b<c<d$ with $a,c$ in one block and $b,d$ in the other. When $u,v$ are adjacent frontier points $i,i+1$, write $J_i$ for $J_{uv}$; these are the noncrossing connectivity states and adjacent-block joins used for planar transfer. The general procedure stores all set partitions when no such annotation is supplied. All arithmetic is exact; each input has finitely many edge updates and finitely many partitions at every frontier.

statement.proposed:
For every finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, integer $Q\geq2$, finite activities $v_e\geq0$, edge order, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, and equivalence relation $\xi$ on $B$, the finite FK connectivity-transfer procedure terminates after finitely many operations and returns exactly
$$Z^\xi_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v)=\sum_{A\subseteq E}Q^{k_\xi(A)}\prod_{e\in A}v_e,$$
where $k_\xi(A)$ counts equivalence classes generated by $\xi$ and the endpoint pairs of occupied edges. In the free case, where $\xi$ is discrete,

statement.proposed:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected simple plane graph, let $F(G)$ be its face set, and choose its unbounded face as the free exterior face. All vertices are free: no boundary vertices are identified or fixed. Fix an integer $Q\geq2$ and finite edge activities $v_e\geq0$. For $A\subseteq E$, write $G_A=(V,A)$ and let $k(A)$ count its connected components, including isolated vertices. Let $G^*$ be the dual multigraph with one vertex for each face and one dual edge $e^*$ crossing each primal edge $e$; loops and parallel edges are retained. Set $A^*:=\{e^*:e\in E\setminus A\}$ and let $k^*(A)$ count the connected components of the spanning dual subgraph $(F(G),A^*)$, counting isolated faces; the unbounded exterior face is one dual vertex counted once.

The medial graph has one four-valent vertex at each primal-dual edge crossing, joined along the corners of the overlay. At each crossing label the four medial half-edges $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$ in cyclic order, with $h_1,h_3$ on the primal-edge sides and $h_2,h_4$ on the dual-edge sides. For $e\in A$, smooth by the noncrossing pairs $(h_4,h_1)$ and $(h_2,h_3)$; for $e\notin A$, smooth by $(h_1,h_2)$ and $(h_3,h_4)$. Equivalently, these curves are the boundary of $N_A$, formed from disjoint small vertex disks and narrow bands along the edges in $A$. Define $\ell(A)$ as the number of connected boundary loops of $N_A$; this also covers a one-vertex graph with no edges. No extra exterior wiring or boundary weight is imposed. Then
$$Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v)=Q^{|V|/2}\sum_{A\subseteq E}(\sqrt Q)^{\ell(A)}\prod_{e\in A}\frac{v_e}{\sqrt Q}.$$
The loop value is $\delta=\sqrt Q$. This is a finite mathematical identity; it asserts no semisimplicity, representation faithfulness, trace, categorification, or empirical claim.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and an integer $N\ge3$. Let $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$, with each coordinate represented by $0,1,\ldots,N-1$, and let $\mathcal E_N$ be the set of unordered nearest-neighbor bonds $\{x,x+e_i\}$, where $1\le i\le d$ and addition is modulo $N$. The condition $N\ge3$ makes this a simple graph with each bond listed once as $x$ ranges over $\Lambda_N$. The site graph is connected because any two coordinate tuples are joined by finitely many steps of $+e_i$ or $-e_i$.

The configuration space is $\Omega_N=\{\eta:\Lambda_N\to\{0,1\}\}$, ordered lexicographically by its binary occupation vector in the fixed site order; this labels it as a finite set $\{1,\ldots,2^{N^d}\}$. The occupation $\eta_x$ is $1$ for an occupied site and $0$ for a vacant site. For $b=\{x,y\}\in\mathcal E_N$, let $\eta^b$ be the configuration obtained by swapping $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$.

The coordinates $x/N$ have dimensionless spacing $1/N$ on the unit torus, and $t$ is dimensionless diffusive time: it is the microscopic unit-rate bond clock accelerated by the factor $N^2$. Thus the continuum heat equation below has normalized diffusion coefficient $D=1$.

Define a rate matrix $L_N$ on $\Omega_N$ by giving each distinct state change $\eta\to\eta^b\ne\eta$ rate $N^2$ and setting the diagonal entry to the negative sum of the off-diagonal row. If the two occupations on a bond agree, swapping them produces no state change and contributes no off-diagonal transition. On a column observable $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb R$, use the row-generator convention $(L_Nf)(\eta)=\sum_{\xi\ne\eta}L_N(\eta,\xi)(f(\xi)-f(\eta))$; a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pL_N$. The **symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)** is the uniformized finite-state chain with rate matrix $L_N$ and any specified initial probability vector. The finite-generator existence result supplies its all-pairs transition matrices $e^{tL_N}$ and càdlàg paths. Every jump conserves $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x$.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N^d$, the fixed-occupancy sector is $\Omega_{N,k}=\{\eta\in\Omega_N:\sum_x\eta_x=k\}$. When $0<k<N^d$, this sector has at least two states and its transition graph is connected by the fixed-occupancy connectivity lemma. Setting every sector energy to $0$, $\beta=1$, and each allowed transition rate to $N^2$ makes this sector a finite reversible stochastic rate model with uniform stationary weights. The sectors $k=0$ and $k=N^d$ are singleton constant chains. The full SSEP state graph is reducible across particle-number sectors; the generic finite rate-matrix construction, not the irreducible reversible-model definition, defines the full process.

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $dx$. For $x\in\Lambda_N$, write $x/N\in\mathbb T^d$ for the point with coordinates represented in $[0,1)$. The empirical measure and its action on a smooth periodic test function $G$ are

$$\pi_t^N:=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)\,\delta_{x/N},\qquad \langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^d}G\,d\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)G(x/N).$$

Here $\delta_y$ denotes unit point mass at $y$. Thus $\pi_t^N$ is a finite positive measure of total mass at most $1$, not necessarily a probability measure. For a smooth periodic $G$, define its discrete Laplacian on grid points by

$$\Delta_NG(x/N):=N^2\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)\bigr].$$

statement.proposed:
Fix a finite nonempty set of states $E$ and a finite time horizon $T\ge0$. A finite-state continuous-time Markov jump process on $[0,T]$ is a family of random elements $X_t$ with values in $E$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. Its paths are constant between successive jump times and take the new state at a jump time (right-continuity); path events use the sigma-algebra generated by the coordinate maps $X_t$. The Markov property here means that, conditional on the history through time $s$, the law of the future path depends on that history only through $(s,X_s)$. For each pair of distinct states $x,y\in E$, its transition rate $\kappa_{xy}:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ is a bounded continuous function. Write

$$\lambda_x(t):=\sum_{y\in E,\ y\ne x}\kappa_{xy}(t).$$

All time integrals without a displayed measure below are oriented Riemann integrals. When a continuous integrand is used as a Lebesgue density, its Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree by the bounded Riemann-integral comparison theorem. The first-jump rate convention is the following. Conditional on the process history through time $s$ and state $X_s=x$, the survival probability of no jump before time $t$, $s\le t\le T$, is

$$H_x(s,t):=\exp\left(-\int_s^t\lambda_x(u)\,du\right).$$

For each $y\ne x$, the conditional density that the next jump occurs at time $t$ and goes to $y$ is $H_x(s,t)\kappa_{xy}(t)$ with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure; the remaining probability $H_x(s,T)$ is that no jump occurs by time $T$. These are normalized conditional probabilities: for $s<T$, by the chain rule and the first fundamental theorem of calculus, $H_x(s,s)=1$ and $H'_x(s,t)=-\lambda_x(t)H_x(s,t)$; the density integrands are continuous, so

$$H_x(s,T)+\sum_{y\ne x}\int_s^T H_x(s,t)\kappa_{xy}(t)\,dt =H_x(s,T)+\int_s^T\lambda_x(t)H_x(s,t)\,dt=1.$$

After each jump the same conditional rule restarts from the new state and jump time. For $s=T$, the next-jump law has unit mass on no further jump. The row generator is the matrix $Q(t)$ with $Q_{xy}(t)=\kappa_{xy}(t)$ for $x\ne y$ and $Q_{xx}(t)=-\lambda_x(t)$. A time-homogeneous process is the special case in which every $\kappa_{xy}(t)$ is constant. When rates carry physical time units, $\kappa_{xy}$ has units of inverse time; this definition is mathematical and asserts no physical realization. The process is called nonexplosive on $[0,T]$ when its path has finitely many jumps there almost surely.

Let $X_t$ be a finite-state continuous-time Markov jump process on $[0,T]$ under the first-jump rate convention, with initial law $\rho$ and bounded continuous rates $\kappa_{xy}(t)$, where $T\ge0$. Put $M:=\sup_{x\in E,\ 0\le t\le T}\lambda_x(t)<\infty$. For $n\ge0$, let $x_0,\ldots,x_n\in E$ with $x_{j-1}\ne x_j$ for $1\le j\le n$, let $0<t_1<\cdots<t_n<T$, and set $t_0:=0$, $t_{n+1}:=T$. Relative to counting measure on state sequences and Lebesgue measure on the ordered time simplex, the probability density of exactly this state sequence and these jump times is

$$\rho(x_0)\left(\prod_{j=1}^n\kappa_{x_{j-1}x_j}(t_j)\right) \exp\left(-\sum_{j=0}^n\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}\lambda_{x_j}(s)\,ds\right).$$

Here an empty product is $1$ and for $n=0$ the formula is $\rho(x_0)\exp(-\int_0^T\lambda_{x_0}(s)\,ds)$; if $T=0$, this is the only path case. For any subinterval $J=[s,t]$ of length $\delta$ with $M\delta<1$, let $N_J$ count its jumps. Then for every integer $n\ge1$,

$$\mathbb P(N_J\ge n)\le(M\delta)^n,\qquad \mathbb E[N_J]\le\frac{M\delta}{1-M\delta}<\infty.$$

If $M=0$ there are no jumps. If $M>0$, divide $[0,T]$ into finitely many intervals with $M\delta<1$; the preceding bound then gives $\mathbb E[N_T]<\infty$. Thus bounded finite-state rates imply nonexplosion on every finite horizon.

Let $p_x(t):=\mathbb P(X_t=x)$ and regard $p(t)$ as a row vector. If $T>0$, then $p$ is continuously differentiable on $(0,T)$ with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and

$$p_y'(t)=\sum_{x\in E,\ x\ne y}p_x(t)\kappa_{xy}(t)-p_y(t)\lambda_y(t),\qquad p'(t)=p(t)Q(t).$$

If $T=0$, the differential assertion is vacuous and the only time marginal is $p(0)$. In either case, if a probability row vector $\pi$ satisfies $\pi Q(t)=0$ for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $p(0)=\pi$, then $p(t)=\pi$ for all $t\in[0,T]$. For constant rates this says that every generator-stationary probability vector is an invariant law of the process.

Let $E$ be a finite nonempty state set, let $q_{xy}\ge0$ be finite time-homogeneous transition rates for distinct $x,y\in E$, and let $Q$ be their row generator. Let $\pi$ be a strictly positive probability row vector with $\pi Q=0$; the forward-equation theorem shows that this is a stationary law when used initially. Assume symmetric support: $q_{xy}>0$ if and only if $q_{yx}>0$. For a sample path on a finite interval $[0,T]$ with successive jump states $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n$, define its stationary path entropy by

$$S_T:=\sum_{j=1}^n\log\left(\frac{\pi_{x_{j-1}}q_{x_{j-1}x_j}}{\pi_{x_j}q_{x_jx_{j-1}}}\right).$$

The bounded-rate path-density lemma shows that the process is nonexplosive on every finite horizon. It also gives zero density to every finite path sequence containing a transition $x\to y$ with $q_{xy}=0$. Since there are countably many finite state sequences, the union of those path strata is null. Hence almost surely the path has finitely many jumps and every jump uses a positive-rate edge. Define $S_T$ by the displayed sum on this full-probability set, and set $S_T=0$ on its null complement, including paths with infinitely many jumps. Every logarithm on the full-probability set is defined because $\pi_x>0$ and symmetric support makes both rates in each jump ratio positive. Its Borel preimages are countable unions of measurable path strata indexed by jump number and finite state sequence, together with the null-complement convention, so $S_T$ is a real random variable. The empty sum for a path with no jumps is $0$. The quantity $S_T$ is dimensionless and depends only on the ordered jump states, not on their times. Detailed balance with respect to $\pi$ means $\pi_xq_{xy}=\pi_yq_{yx}$ for every pair $x\ne y$; under this condition each jump contribution is zero, but no detailed-balance condition is part of this definition.

$$G_y(t):=\mathbb E\left[\exp\left(-\int_0^t V_{X_s}(s)\,ds\right)\mathbf 1_{\{X_t=y\}}\right].$$

Then $G(0)=\rho$. If $T>0$, $G$ is continuously differentiable on $(0,T)$ with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and it is the unique solution of

$$G_y'(t)=\sum_{x\ne y}G_x(t)\kappa_{xy}(t)-G_y(t)\lambda_y(t)-V_y(t)G_y(t).$$

If $T=0$, the unique function on the singleton time interval is $G(0)=\rho$, and no differential equation is asserted.

statement.proposed:
Let $E$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $q_{xy}\ge0$ be finite time-homogeneous transition rates for $x\ne y$. Put $\lambda_x:=\sum_{y\ne x}q_{xy}$. Assume the positive-rate graph is irreducible (every ordered pair of states is joined by a finite directed path of positive-rate edges), the rates have symmetric support $q_{xy}>0$ if and only if $q_{yx}>0$, and $\pi$ is a strictly positive probability row vector satisfying $\pi Q=0$ for the row generator $Q$. The forward equation shows that $\pi$ is a stationary law when used as the initial distribution. Start the process with law $\pi$, and define $S_T$ by the stationary path-entropy definition for any finite nonnegative horizon $T$.

For every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, the path law and its time reversal obey

$$\mathbb P(S_T\in B)=\int_{-B}e^{-u}\,\mu_T(du),\qquad \mathbb E[e^{-S_T}]=1,\qquad \mathbb E[S_T]\ge0,$$

where $\mu_T(C):=\mathbb P(S_T\in C)$ and $-B:=\{-s:s\in B\}$. Equivalently, as a measure identity, $\mu_T(ds)=e^s\mu_T(-ds)$. The identity is exact at finite time and does not assume that $\mu_T$ has a density.

statement.proposed:
Let $E$ be a finite nonempty state set and $T\ge0$. Fix $\beta>0$. If $T>0$, for each $x\in E$ let $E_x\in C^1([0,T],\mathbb R)$ be an energy function; if $T=0$, let each $E_x(0)$ be finite. Let $\kappa_{xy}:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded continuous transition rates for $x\ne y$, and let $X_t$ be the associated finite-state Markov jump process. Define

$$Z_t:=\sum_{x\in E}e^{-\beta E_x(t)},\qquad \pi_t(x):=\frac{e^{-\beta E_x(t)}}{Z_t}.$$

Assume instantaneous detailed balance:

$$\pi_t(x)\kappa_{xy}(t)=\pi_t(y)\kappa_{yx}(t)\qquad(x\ne y,\ 0\le t\le T),$$

and initial law $\mathbb P(X_0=x)=\pi_0(x)$. The path work and free-energy difference are

$$W_T:=\begin{cases}0,&T=0,\\ \int_0^T E'_{X_t}(t)\,dt,&T>0,\end{cases}\qquad \Delta F:=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_T/Z_0).$$

Then

$$\mathbb E[e^{-\beta W_T}]=\frac{Z_T}{Z_0}=e^{-\beta\Delta F}.$$

If energy is measured in joules, then $\beta$ has units $\mathrm J^{-1}$, $W_T$ and $\Delta F$ have units joules, and the exponent is dimensionless. Under a common $C^1$ energy shift $E_x(t)\mapsto E_x(t)+a(t)$ for all $x$, both $W_T$ and $\Delta F$ change by $a(T)-a(0)$, so the identity is unchanged.

statement.proposed:
Let $N\ge3$ be an integer and let the state space be the ring $E=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. From state $i$, let the constant clockwise rate to $i+1$ be $a>0$ and the counterclockwise rate to $i-1$ be $b>0$, with all other off-diagonal rates zero. Start the finite-state process in the uniform law $\pi_i=1/N$. If $N_+$ and $N_-$ denote the numbers of clockwise and counterclockwise jumps on $[0,T]$, then $\pi$ is stationary and, almost surely, the stationary path entropy is

$$S_T=(N_+-N_-)\log(a/b).$$

Its mean is $\mathbb E[S_T]=T(a-b)\log(a/b)\ge0$. Reversibility here means detailed balance with respect to the stationary law; it holds exactly when $a=b$. For every finite $T\ge0$, this ring also satisfies the exact measure fluctuation relation $\mu_T(ds)=e^s\mu_T(-ds)$, where $\mu_T$ is the law of $S_T$. If $a,b$ are physical rates, they have units of inverse time; $aT,bT$ and $S_T$ are dimensionless.

Input a finite nonempty set $V$, a set $E\subseteq[V]^2$ of unordered pairs of distinct sites, finite dimensionless couplings $K_e\geq0$, finite dimensionless fields $h_i\in\mathbb R$, and a two-sided iid stream $(I_s,U_s)_{s\in\mathbb Z}$ in which $I_s$ is uniform on $V$, $U_s$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, and all these variables are mutually independent. The spin space is $\Omega=\{-1,+1\}^V$ with coordinatewise order, minimum $\mathbf{-}$ and maximum $\mathbf{+}$. In the categorical sampler of [[alg-csm-frontier-heat-bath-update]], use the fixed total order $+1\prec-1$; this sampler order is separate from the coordinatewise spin order. Define the strictly positive finite weight
$$w(\sigma)=\exp\!\left(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}K_{\{i,j\}}\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sum_{i\in V}h_i\sigma_i\right).$$
At time $s$, let $F_s:\Omega\to\Omega$ be the heat-bath update from [[alg-csm-frontier-heat-bath-update]] using site $I_s$ and uniform $U_s$; in particular, site $i$ is set to $+1$ exactly when
$$U_s<\frac{\exp(H_i(\eta))}{\exp(H_i(\eta))+\exp(-H_i(\eta))},\qquad H_i(\eta)=h_i+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}K_{\{i,j\}}\eta_j,$$
where $\eta$ is the exterior configuration at $i$, and otherwise is set to $-1$. For $T=1,2,4,\ldots$, initialize lower and upper configurations at time $-T$ to $\mathbf{-}$ and $\mathbf{+}$, respectively, and apply in chronological order the same stored maps $F_{-T+1},\ldots,F_0$ to both. If their time-zero outputs agree, return that common configuration. Otherwise double $T$ and replay all maps in the enlarged interval, reusing the already stored maps at every overlapping time. This is a random procedure; no finite running-time bound is part of its definition.

$$U_s<\frac{\exp(H_i(\eta))}{\exp(H_i(\eta))+\exp(-H_i(\eta))},\qquad H_i(\eta)=h_i+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}K_{\{i,j\}}\eta_j,$$
where $\eta$ is the exterior configuration at $i$, and otherwise is set to $-1$. For $T=1,2,4,\ldots$, initialize lower and upper configurations at time $-T$ to $\mathbf{-}$ and $\mathbf{+}$, respectively, and apply in chronological order the same stored maps $F_{-T+1},\ldots,F_0$ to both.
